prompt.context: Our client is a public university that is considering adding an inter-collegiate football team to its athletic program. They have asked us to help them determine if this is a good idea. The school has an enrollment of 10,000 students and is located near a city of 1 million residents in the Southern US where football is very popular. The school currently participates in 16 men's and women's sports including basketball, track & field, and baseball. The school feels that adding a football program has many benefits including increased exposure and brand awareness, school pride, enhanced college experience for students, improved connections with alumni, and additional revenue. Their only financial requirement is to break even. Longer term, they hope to pay for a new stadium and use football to subsidize other sports programs on campus.
prompt.question: Should the university add an inter-collegiate football program? Specifically, can the program break even financially in Year 1?

clarifying_info.a: Southern US, near a city of 1 million residents

clarifying_info.q: What sports does the school currently offer?
clarifying_info.a: 16 men's and women's sports including basketball, track & field, and baseball
Break even — they are primarily interested in the intangible benefits (exposure, school pride, alumni connections, student experience)

clarifying_info.q: What are the expected revenue sources?
clarifying_info.a: Student fees, game guarantees for away games, ticket sales, and alumni support

clarifying_info.q: How many home and away games are expected?
What ticket price and expected attendance?
clarifying_info.a: $25 per ticket per home game; expected attendance of 7,000 per game in season 1 (excluding students)

clarifying_info.q: What student fee increase is expected?
clarifying_info.a: $250 per student per year (combination of tuition and student fee increases)

clarifying_info.q: What game guarantees are expected for away games?
How many scholarship players will there be?
clarifying_info.a: 52 scholarship players; financial aid covers tuition/fees ($14K/year), room & board ($12K/year), and books ($2K/year) per player
Head coach: $500K/year; 8 assistant coaches at $125K/year each

clarifying_info.q: What are the support staff costs?
clarifying_info.a: 25 new employees at an average cost of $60K/year

clarifying_info.q: What are equipment and uniform costs?
clarifying_info.a: $1,500 per player per year for 80 total players
The school can rent a small stadium from the city for $100K per home game

framework: Revenue analysis: Identify and quantify all revenue streams (student fees, ticket sales, game guarantees, alumni support, concessions, broadcasting rights, apparel/licensing)
Cost analysis: Break down costs into capital costs and operating costs (coaching & staff salaries, stadium costs, equipment/uniforms, travel, financial aid/scholarships, recruiting)
Break-even analysis: Compare total revenues to total costs and determine if the program meets the client's financial requirement
Intangibles: Assess non-financial benefits (brand awareness, school pride, student experience, alumni engagement, long-term subsidy of other sports)
Stadium decision (Part 2): Evaluate incremental revenues and costs of building a new on-campus stadium; determine if conference membership benefits justify the investment
Risk assessment: Identify key assumptions and risks (attendance, alumni donations, cost overruns)

questions.prompt: Calculate total Year 1 revenues for the football program.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify all four revenue streams and calculate each. Strong candidates will proactively ask about each category. The total should come to $6.35M.

math.setup: Four revenue streams: student fees, game guarantees, ticket sales, alumni support
steps: Ticket Sales: $25/ticket x 6 home games x 7,000 attendees = $1,050,000

questions.prompt: Calculate total Year 1 operating costs for the football program.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify all major cost categories and calculate each. Strong candidates will ask about financial aid, salaries, travel, recruiting, equipment, and stadium rental separately. Total should come to $5.9M (or ~$5.856M precise).

math.setup: Six cost categories: financial aid, salaries, travel, recruiting, equipment, stadium rental

questions.prompt: Based on your revenue and cost calculations, can the program break even in Year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare $6.35M revenue to $5.9M costs. The program shows a surplus of approximately $450K–$494K, which satisfies the break-even requirement. Strong candidates note this is barely break-even and highly sensitive to attendance and alumni support assumptions.

math.setup: Compare total revenue to total costs
math.answer: Yes, the program can break even in Year 1 with a surplus of approximately $450K–$494K

questions.prompt: The team has had surprising success and a more powerful athletic conference has invited the school to join, but they need a bigger stadium. The client wants to build a 25,000-seat on-campus stadium at a cost of $40M. Is this a good idea?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate incremental revenues and incremental costs of the new stadium and compare. The net result is an incremental loss of $500K/year, meaning the program cannot justify the stadium without additional revenue (e.g., a conference revenue guarantee). Strong candidates ask about financing terms before calculating.

math.setup: Calculate incremental ticket revenue from new stadium, then subtract incremental costs (loan repayment + higher operating costs)
steps: New stadium capacity: 25,000 seats x 80% occupancy = 20,000 attendees per game
Students attending free: 50% x 10,000 students = 5,000 students per game
Paid attendance per game: 20,000 - 5,000 = 15,000 paying fans
Annual paid attendance: 15,000 x 6 home games = 90,000
Incremental costs — higher operating costs: $100,000/game x 6 games = $600,000/year
math.answer: The stadium creates an incremental loss of $500K/year. The school would need at least $500K/year in additional revenue (e.g., from the new conference) to justify building it.

brainstorming.prompt: Can you think of additional ways to make the football program more profitable?

categories.name: Revenue — Sponsorship & Media
ideas: Negotiate higher game guarantees for away games

categories.name: Revenue — Apparel & Licensing
ideas: Work with uniform/apparel companies to secure free uniforms or licensing deals
Apparel licensing and sales to fans and alumni

categories.name: Revenue — Game Day
ideas: Sell season ticket packages before the season starts
Rent the stadium out for non-football events (concerts, other sports)

categories.name: Revenue — Enrollment & Alumni
ideas: Increased football visibility may lead to higher student enrollment (indirectly increasing tuition revenue)
Use football profile to strengthen alumni fundraising campaigns

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Structure coaching compensation to be performance-based (lower base, higher bonus)
Use external marketing firm to increase demand and optimize pricing

recommendation: The university should proceed with starting a football program. The program can break even in Year 1 under the given assumptions, satisfying the client's only financial requirement. Beyond financials, the program delivers meaningful intangible benefits: increased exposure and brand awareness, enhanced student experience, stronger alumni connections, and a platform to subsidize other sports programs long-term.

The client should be cautious about building an on-campus stadium. Under current assumptions, the new stadium generates an incremental loss of $500K/year and should not be pursued unless the school receives reasonable assurances of at least $500K in additional annual revenue — for example, a guaranteed conference revenue share from joining the new athletic conference.
risks: Attendance in Year 1 may be lower than the assumed 7,000 per game, which would erode the slim break-even margin
Alumni donations of $1M/year may be difficult to sustain, especially early in the program's life
Stadium construction costs could exceed the $40M estimate
The new conference membership benefit is not guaranteed; without it, the stadium is a money-losing investment
next_steps: Verify financial assumptions and assign workstreams to validate revenue and cost estimates
Begin recruiting a head football coach immediately — coach quality will drive early success and attendance
Publicize plans with prominent alumni to begin soliciting donations
Initiate the process of increasing student fees
Start talks with the city to arrange use of the rented stadium for home games
Sell season ticket packages before the first season to lock in early revenue
For the stadium: continue renting or explore partnering with the city to build a multi-purpose stadium, which would spread costs and enable non-football revenue
